topics.title: Propositional Logic
topics.definition: Propositional logic studies statements that are either true or false and how they combine.

children.title: Propositions and truth values
children.definition: A proposition is a declarative statement with a definite truth value, such as "2 + 2 = 4".

children.title: Logical connectives
children.definition: Negation, conjunction, disjunction, exclusive or, implication and biconditional.

children.title: Truth tables
children.definition: A table listing the truth value of a compound statement for every combination of its variables.

children.title: Tautology, contradiction and contingency
children.definition: Always true, always false and sometimes true statements respectively.

children.title: Logical equivalence and laws
children.definition: Identity, domination, idempotent, double negation, commutative, associative, distributive, De Morgan and absorption laws.

children.title: Normal forms
children.definition: Conjunctive and disjunctive normal forms, and functional completeness of the connectives.

children.title: Arguments and validity
children.definition: An argument is valid when the conclusion must be true whenever all premises are true.

card.explanation: A proposition is a statement that is definitely true or definitely false, such as two plus two equals four. Connectives join propositions into larger ones: negation, conjunction, disjunction, exclusive or, implication and biconditional. A truth table lists the value of the whole statement for every combination of the variables. A statement that is always true is a tautology, one that is always false is a contradiction, and the rest are contingencies. Two statements are logically equivalent when their truth table columns match. The laws of De Morgan, distribution and absorption are used to rewrite one into the other.
card.example: The statement it is raining or it is not raining is a tautology, because one half must hold. The statement it is raining and it is not raining is a contradiction.

quiz.q: Which connective gives a true result only when both inputs are true?
quiz.why: Conjunction, the and operator, is true only when both of its operands are true.

quiz.q: A statement that is true for every combination of its variables is called:
quiz.why: A tautology is always true, a contradiction is always false, and a contingency is sometimes each.

quiz.q: Which statement about propositional logic is NOT correct?
options: A truth table lists every combination of the variables
De Morgan laws relate conjunction, disjunction and negation
An implication is true only when both of its parts are true
A proposition has a definite truth value
quiz.why: An implication is false only when the premise is true and the conclusion is false.

quiz.q: How many rows does a truth table for three variables have?
quiz.why: Each variable doubles the count, so three variables give 2 to the power 3, which is 8 rows.

quiz.q: An argument whose conclusion must be true whenever all its premises are true is called:
quiz.why: Validity is about the link from premises to conclusion; soundness also needs the premises to be true.

card.examTip: Write the six connectives with their symbols, then draw one truth table and label the tautology and the contradiction.

topics.title: Predicates and Quantifiers
topics.definition: Predicate logic extends propositional logic with variables, predicates and quantifiers.

children.title: Predicates
children.definition: A statement involving variables, such as P(x) meaning x is greater than 3, which becomes a proposition when x is fixed.

children.title: Universal quantifier
children.definition: For all x, written with an upside down A, true when P(x) holds for every element of the domain.

children.title: Existential quantifier
children.definition: There exists an x, written with a backwards E, true when at least one element satisfies P(x).

children.title: Negating quantified statements
children.definition: The negation of for all is there exists a counterexample, and the negation of there exists is for all not.

children.title: Nested quantifiers
children.definition: Statements such as for all x there exists y, where the order of quantifiers changes the meaning.

children.title: Rules of inference
children.definition: Modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, disjunctive syllogism, addition, simplification, conjunction and resolution.

children.title: Fallacies
children.definition: The fallacy of affirming the consequent and of denying the antecedent, which look valid but are not.

card.explanation: A predicate is a statement with a variable in it, such as P of x meaning x is greater than three. It becomes a proposition only once the variable is given a value or bound by a quantifier. The universal quantifier says that P holds for every element of the domain, and the existential quantifier says it holds for at least one. Negation flips them: not for all becomes there exists a counterexample, and not there exists becomes for all not. With nested quantifiers the order matters, because for all x there exists y says something different from there exists y for all x.
card.example: For every student there is a subject they like is not the same as there is a subject that every student likes. Swapping the two quantifiers changes what is being claimed.

quiz.q: Which quantifier says that a predicate holds for every element of the domain?
quiz.why: The universal quantifier, written as an upside down A, claims the predicate for all elements.

quiz.q: What is the negation of the statement every student passed?
options: At least one student did not pass
quiz.why: Negating a universal gives an existential, because one counterexample is enough to break the claim.

quiz.q: Which statement about quantifiers is NOT correct?
options: A predicate becomes a proposition once its variable is bound
The order of nested quantifiers can change the meaning
The negation of there exists is for all not
For all x there exists y means the same as there exists y for all x
quiz.why: The first says each x has its own y, while the second says one single y works for every x.

quiz.q: Which of these is a valid rule of inference?
quiz.why: Modus ponens takes p and p implies q and concludes q; the other three are known fallacies.

quiz.q: Which argument form is a fallacy?
quiz.why: From p implies q and q you cannot conclude p, because q may hold for another reason.

card.examTip: Write the two quantifiers with their symbols, give the two negation rules, then show why swapping nested quantifiers changes the meaning.

topics.title: Methods of Proof
topics.definition: A proof is a valid argument that establishes the truth of a mathematical statement.

children.title: Direct proof
children.definition: Assume the hypothesis and derive the conclusion by known facts and algebra.

children.title: Indirect proof by contraposition
children.definition: Prove the contrapositive, that not q implies not p, which is logically equivalent to p implies q.

children.title: Proof by contradiction
children.definition: Assume the statement is false and derive a contradiction, used classically to prove the irrationality of the square root of 2.

children.title: Vacuous and trivial proof
children.definition: A conditional is vacuously true when the hypothesis is false and trivially true when the conclusion is known to be true.

children.title: Proof by cases and exhaustive proof
children.definition: Split the statement into covering cases and prove each one.

children.title: Existence and uniqueness proofs
children.definition: Show that an object exists, and if required that it is the only one.

children.title: Constructive versus non constructive proof
children.definition: Either produce the object or prove it must exist without producing it.

card.explanation: A proof is a valid argument that leaves no doubt about a statement. A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and works forward with known facts until the conclusion appears. Proof by contraposition proves not q implies not p instead, which is logically the same claim. Proof by contradiction assumes the statement is false and derives something impossible, the classic example being that the square root of two is irrational. A proof by cases splits the statement into cases that cover everything, and an existence proof shows that at least one object exists.
card.example: To prove that if n squared is odd then n is odd, prove the contrapositive instead. If n is even then n squared is even, which follows at once.

quiz.q: Which method proves not q implies not p instead of p implies q?
quiz.why: A conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent, so proving one proves the other.

quiz.q: Which classical result is proved by contradiction in most textbooks?
options: The sum of the first n integers
The irrationality of the square root of two
quiz.why: Assuming the square root of two is rational forces a common factor, which contradicts the fraction being in lowest terms.

quiz.q: Which statement about proofs is NOT correct?
options: A proof by cases only needs to cover the largest case
A vacuous proof relies on the hypothesis being false
A trivial proof relies on the conclusion being already known
A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and derives the conclusion
quiz.why: The cases must exhaust every possibility, or a gap remains where the statement is unproved.

quiz.q: Which proof shows an object exists without producing it?
quiz.why: A constructive proof hands you the object, while a non constructive one only shows that it must exist.

quiz.q: How many cases must a proof by cases cover?
options: As many as there are words in the theorem
Every case that the statement allows
quiz.why: The cases have to be exhaustive, otherwise the statement stays unproved in the gap.

card.examTip: Name each method in one line with the shape of its argument, and keep the square root of two ready for the contradiction method.

topics.title: Proof Strategies and Mathematical Induction
topics.definition: Strategies guide which proof method to try, and induction proves statements about all natural numbers.

children.title: Forward and backward reasoning
children.definition: Work from the hypothesis towards the goal, or from the goal backwards to known facts.

children.title: Adapting an existing proof and looking for counterexamples
children.definition: Reuse known proofs with modifications, and test small cases before attempting a proof.

children.title: Principle of mathematical induction
children.definition: Prove the base case and the inductive step that P(k) implies P(k + 1), which proves P(n) for all n.

children.title: Strong induction and well ordering
children.definition: Strong induction assumes all smaller cases, and the well ordering property says every non-empty set of positive integers has a least element.

children.title: Common induction mistakes
children.definition: Assuming what is to be proved and skipping the base case.

card.explanation: Strategy is about choosing a method before writing a line. Work forward from the hypothesis, or work backward from the goal until it meets a known fact. Try small cases first, because a counterexample found early saves a long attempt at a proof. Induction proves a statement for every natural number in two steps. The base case is proved first, then the step showing that P of k implies P of k plus one. Strong induction assumes all the smaller cases instead of only the previous one. The well ordering property is why induction works at all.
card.example: To prove the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared, check n equals 1. Then show that adding the next odd number takes k squared to k plus one squared.

quiz.q: What are the two steps of a proof by mathematical induction?
quiz.why: The base case starts the chain and the inductive step keeps it going for every natural number.

quiz.q: How does strong induction differ from ordinary induction?
options: It assumes the statement for all smaller values
It proves the statement for real numbers
quiz.why: Strong induction may use any earlier case, which helps when the step depends on more than one predecessor.

quiz.q: Which statement about induction is NOT correct?
options: The well ordering property underlies induction
Assuming the conclusion and reaching a known fact is a valid inductive step
The base case must be proved separately
The inductive step proves P of k implies P of k plus one
quiz.why: Assuming what you are proving is circular, and it is the most common induction mistake.

quiz.q: Which mistake breaks an induction proof?
options: Proving the inductive step in detail
quiz.why: Without a base case the chain has nothing to start from, so nothing at all is proved.

quiz.q: What does the well ordering property say?
options: Every set has a largest element
Every non-empty set of positive integers has a least element
quiz.why: That least element is what makes the descent argument behind induction and strong induction work.

card.examTip: Write the two induction steps as labelled lines, then add one sentence on the two usual mistakes: no base case and assuming the conclusion.

topics.title: Sets
topics.definition: A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects called its elements.

children.title: Set builder and roster notation
children.definition: Sets are listed as {1, 2, 3} or described as {x | x is an even integer}.

children.title: Subsets and power set
children.definition: A is a subset of B if every element of A is in B; the power set is the set of all subsets and has 2 to the n elements.

children.title: Set operations
children.definition: Union, intersection, difference, complement and symmetric difference.

children.title: Set identities and Venn diagrams
children.definition: Algebraic identities such as De Morgan laws together with diagrams that show operations visually.

children.title: Cardinality and inclusion exclusion
children.definition: The size of a set, with the two set rule |A union B| = |A| + |B| - |A intersection B|.

children.title: Cartesian product and ordered pairs
children.definition: The set of all ordered pairs from two sets, which underlies relations and functions.

card.explanation: A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects, listed or given by a rule such as x such that x is even. A is a subset of B when every element of A also lies in B, and the power set holds all the subsets. The operations are union, intersection, difference, complement and symmetric difference, and the identities they obey mirror the laws of logic. The size of a set is its cardinality, and the inclusion exclusion rule stops the overlap being counted twice. The Cartesian product collects every ordered pair from two sets, which is what relations and functions are built on.
card.example: A set of three students has 2 to the power 3, which is 8 subsets in its power set. That already takes a line to list, which is why the power set grows too fast to write out for large sets.

quiz.q: How many subsets does a set with 4 elements have?
quiz.why: The power set has 2 to the power n elements, so 2 to the power 4 gives 16.

quiz.q: Which rule gives the size of the union of two overlapping sets?
quiz.why: Inclusion exclusion subtracts the intersection once, because those elements were counted twice.

quiz.q: Which statement about sets is NOT correct?
options: The order of elements in a set does not matter
The empty set is a subset of every set
The power set of A has the same number of elements as A
A set lists each element only once
quiz.why: The power set has 2 to the power n elements, which is larger than n for every non-empty set.

quiz.q: If A has 10 elements, B has 7 and their intersection has 3, what is the size of the union?
quiz.why: Inclusion exclusion gives 10 + 7 - 3, which is 14.

quiz.q: What does the Cartesian product of A and B contain?
options: Every ordered pair with the first from A and the second from B
Only the elements common to A and B
The subsets shared by A and B
Every element of A plus every element of B
quiz.why: Ordered pairs are what make relations and functions possible, and the order inside each pair matters.

card.examTip: Write the set operations with their symbols, then give the inclusion exclusion formula and one worked example with numbers.

topics.title: Functions
topics.definition: A function maps each element of its domain to exactly one element of its codomain.

children.title: Domain, codomain and range
children.definition: The allowed inputs, the declared output set and the outputs actually produced.

children.title: Injective (one to one) function
children.definition: Different inputs always give different outputs.

children.title: Surjective (onto) function
children.definition: Every element of the codomain is the image of some input.

children.title: Bijective function and inverse
children.definition: Both injective and surjective, so an inverse function exists.

children.title: Composition and graphs of functions
children.definition: Composition applies one function after another, and the graph shows the ordered pairs.

children.title: Important functions
children.definition: Identity, constant, floor, ceiling, factorial and exponential functions.

card.explanation: A function takes each element of its domain and gives back exactly one element of its codomain. The domain is the set of allowed inputs, the codomain is the declared output set and the range is what actually comes out. A function is injective when different inputs always give different outputs, and surjective when every element of the codomain is reached. A function that is both is bijective, and only then does an inverse exist. Composition applies one function after another, and the graph of a function is the set of its ordered pairs.
card.example: The function that squares an integer is not injective, because 2 and minus 2 both give 4. Restricting the domain to non-negative integers makes it injective, and then an inverse exists.

quiz.q: What is a function that is both injective and surjective called?
quiz.why: Bijective means one to one and onto, which is exactly when an inverse function exists.

quiz.q: Which statement about functions is NOT correct?
options: An injective function never sends two inputs to the same output
A surjective function reaches every element of the codomain
Every input maps to exactly one output
quiz.why: An inverse needs the function to be bijective, and most functions are not.

quiz.q: The range of a function is:
options: The set of outputs actually produced
quiz.why: The codomain is what is declared up front; the range is the part of it that is really hit.

quiz.q: A function from a set of 3 elements to a set of 5 elements cannot be:
quiz.why: Three inputs produce at most three outputs, so two elements of the codomain are missed.

quiz.q: What does the composition of two functions do?
options: Applies one function and then the other
quiz.why: Composition feeds the output of one function straight into the input of the next.

card.examTip: Draw two small arrow diagrams, one injective and one surjective, and write the one line condition for each.

topics.title: Sequences and Sums
topics.definition: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers and a sum adds the terms of a sequence.

children.title: Arithmetic progression
children.definition: Each term differs from the previous one by a constant, with sum n over 2 times first plus last.

children.title: Geometric progression
children.definition: Each term is a constant multiple of the previous one, with sum a(r to the n minus 1) over (r minus 1).

children.title: Recurrence relations
children.definition: A sequence defined by earlier terms, such as the Fibonacci relation.

children.title: Special integer sequences
children.definition: Fibonacci numbers, factorials, powers and triangular numbers.

children.title: Summation notation and formulas
children.definition: Sigma notation, sums of constants, arithmetic series, geometric series and sums of squares and cubes.

card.explanation: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers following a rule, and a series adds its terms. In an arithmetic progression each term differs from the previous one by a constant. Its sum is n over 2 times the first term plus the last. In a geometric progression each term is a fixed multiple of the previous one, and the sum formula divides by r minus 1. A recurrence relation defines a term from earlier terms, as the Fibonacci rule does. Sigma notation writes a sum compactly, and the formulas for the first n integers, squares and cubes save pages of arithmetic.
card.example: Saving 100 rupees more each month than the last gives an arithmetic progression. The total after a year is 12 over 2 times the first month plus the last month's amount.

quiz.q: What is the sum of the first 100 positive integers?
quiz.why: The formula n times n plus 1 over 2 gives 100 times 101 over 2, which is 5,050.

quiz.q: In a geometric progression, each term is:
options: The sum of the two previous terms
quiz.why: A fixed multiplier defines a geometric progression, while a fixed difference defines an arithmetic one.

quiz.q: Which statement about sequences is NOT correct?
options: Every recurrence relation has a closed form that is easy to find
An arithmetic progression has a constant difference
The Fibonacci sequence is defined by a recurrence
A geometric progression has a constant ratio
quiz.why: Many recurrences have no simple closed form, which is why they are studied in their own right.

quiz.q: Which sequence is defined by adding the two previous terms?
quiz.why: The Fibonacci rule takes each term as the sum of the two before it, once the first two are fixed.

quiz.q: What is the sum of the arithmetic progression 2, 5, 8, 11, 14?
quiz.why: There are 5 terms, so the sum is 5 over 2 times 2 plus 14, which is 40.

card.examTip: Write the two progression formulas side by side, then add the sigma formulas for the first n integers, squares and cubes.

topics.title: Matrices
topics.definition: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers used to represent data and transformations.

children.title: Matrix types
children.definition: Row, column, square, diagonal, identity, symmetric and zero matrices.

children.title: Matrix operations
children.definition: Addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication and matrix multiplication with its row by column rule.

children.title: Transpose and trace
children.definition: The transpose swaps rows and columns and the trace adds the diagonal elements.

children.title: Inverse of a matrix
children.definition: Exists only for square matrices with non-zero determinant, with A times inverse equals identity.

children.title: Boolean matrices
children.definition: Entries are 0 and 1 with the join and meet operations, used to represent relations.

card.explanation: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. It may be square, diagonal, symmetric, an identity matrix or a zero matrix, depending on its shape and its entries. Matrices of the same size add and subtract entry by entry, and multiplication follows the row by column rule. The transpose swaps rows with columns, and the trace adds the entries on the main diagonal. A square matrix has an inverse only when its determinant is not zero. A Boolean matrix uses only 0 and 1, with join and meet as its operations.
card.example: Multiplying a 2 by 3 matrix by a 3 by 4 matrix gives a 2 by 4 result. The inner dimensions must match, or the product is not defined.

quiz.q: When can two matrices be multiplied?
options: When both have the same determinant
When they have the same number of rows
When the columns of the first equal the rows of the second
quiz.why: The inner dimensions must match, and the result takes the two outer dimensions.

quiz.q: What is the trace of a matrix?
options: The sum of the entries on the main diagonal
The product of all its entries
quiz.why: The trace is defined only for a square matrix, and it adds the diagonal entries.

quiz.q: Which statement about matrices is NOT correct?
options: The transpose swaps rows and columns
An inverse exists only when the determinant is non-zero
An identity matrix has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere
quiz.why: Order matters in matrix multiplication, so A times B usually differs from B times A.

quiz.q: A 2 by 3 matrix is multiplied by a 3 by 5 matrix. What is the size of the result?
quiz.why: The inner dimensions 3 and 3 match, and the result takes the outer dimensions 2 and 5.

quiz.q: What values does a Boolean matrix hold?
quiz.why: Boolean matrices use 0 and 1 with join and meet, which is how relations are stored.

card.examTip: Give the row by column rule in one line, then state the condition for an inverse and the shape rule for a product.

topics.title: Relations
topics.definition: A relation from A to B is a subset of the Cartesian product A cross B.

children.title: Binary relations and their representation
children.definition: Sets of ordered pairs shown as lists, matrices or directed graphs.

children.title: Properties of relations
children.definition: Reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive and irreflexive on a set.

children.title: Equivalence relations
children.definition: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive; they partition the set into equivalence classes.

children.title: Partial ordering relations
children.definition: Reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; Hasse diagrams draw them compactly, with maximal, minimal, least and greatest elements.

children.title: Closures of relations
children.definition: The reflexive, symmetric and transitive closure, with Warshall algorithm for transitive closure.

children.title: n-ary relations and databases
children.definition: Relations of degree n as tables, with primary keys as candidate keys and operations like selection and projection.

card.explanation: A relation from A to B is any subset of the Cartesian product A cross B, so it is a set of ordered pairs. It can be written as a list of pairs, as a zero one matrix or as a directed graph. On a single set a relation may be reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric or transitive, and which of these hold decides what the relation is called. A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive is an equivalence relation, and it cuts the set into equivalence classes. One that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive is a partial order, drawn as a Hasse diagram.
card.example: Equality is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation. The divides relation on the positive integers is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, so it is a partial order.

quiz.q: Which three properties make a relation an equivalence relation?
quiz.why: Those three together are what partitions the set into equivalence classes.

quiz.q: Which properties define a partial order?
quiz.why: Antisymmetry replaces symmetry, which lets a partial order compare elements rather than group them.

quiz.q: Which statement about relations is NOT correct?
options: A relation can be stored as a zero one matrix
The transitive closure is computed by Warshall algorithm
Every reflexive relation is also symmetric
A relation can be drawn as a directed graph
quiz.why: Reflexive and symmetric are independent properties, and neither one follows from the other.

quiz.q: What does the reflexive closure of a relation add?
options: Every pair reachable by a path
Nothing, because closures only remove pairs
Every missing pair a to a
quiz.why: The reflexive closure adds self loops, the symmetric one adds reverses and the transitive one adds path shortcuts.

quiz.q: Which algorithm computes the transitive closure of a relation?
quiz.why: Warshall works on the relation matrix and fills in every pair reachable by a path.

card.examTip: List the five properties with a one line test for each, then give the property sets for equivalence and for partial order.

topics.title: Divisibility and Modular Arithmetic
topics.definition: Divisibility studies when one integer divides another exactly, and modular arithmetic keeps only remainders.

children.title: Division algorithm and divisibility
children.definition: For integers a and d with d positive there are unique q and r with a = dq + r and 0 <= r < d; d divides a if r is 0.

children.title: Congruence modulo m
children.definition: a is congruent to b mod m when m divides a minus b, which means both leave the same remainder.

children.title: Arithmetic modulo m
children.definition: Addition and multiplication wrap around using the remainder, which models clocks and hashing.

children.title: Applications of modular arithmetic
children.definition: Hash functions, check digits, day of the week arithmetic and cryptography.

children.title: Linear congruences
children.definition: Equations ax congruent to b mod m, solvable when the gcd of a and m divides b.

card.explanation: The division algorithm says that a equals d times q plus r, with r between zero and d minus one. Both q and r are unique. When r is zero we say d divides a. Congruence modulo m means that m divides a minus b, which is the same as saying a and b leave the same remainder. Addition and multiplication can be done on the remainders, and the answer is taken modulo m again. That wrapping is what makes clocks, hash tables and check digits work. A linear congruence a x congruent to b modulo m has a solution exactly when the gcd of a and m divides b.
card.example: If it is 10 o'clock now, then in 5 hours it is 3 o'clock. The reason is that 15 modulo 12 is 3.

quiz.q: What does it mean to say a is congruent to b modulo m?
options: a and b are both prime
quiz.why: Congruence means the difference is a multiple of m, so both numbers leave the same remainder.

quiz.q: What is 17 modulo 5?
quiz.why: 17 is 3 times 5 plus 2, so the remainder is 2.

quiz.q: Which statement about modular arithmetic is NOT correct?
options: Clocks are an example of arithmetic modulo 12
Every non-zero element has an inverse modulo any m
quiz.why: An inverse exists only when a and m are coprime, which is why prime moduli matter in cryptography.

quiz.q: When does the linear congruence a x congruent to b modulo m have a solution?
options: When the gcd of a and m divides b
Only when a and m are coprime
quiz.why: The gcd condition decides solvability, and the number of solutions equals that gcd.

quiz.q: In the division algorithm a = dq + r, what range does r lie in?
quiz.why: The remainder is non-negative and strictly smaller than the divisor, which is what makes q and r unique.

card.examTip: State the division algorithm with the range of r, define congruence, then give one clock sum and one hash example.

topics.title: Integer Algorithms
topics.definition: Classical algorithms work on integers and many of them run in time proportional to the number of digits.

children.title: Integer representation and base conversion
children.definition: Numbers in base b are converted to decimal by expansion and back by repeated division.

children.title: Euclidean algorithm for GCD
children.definition: Repeatedly replace the pair by the divisor and remainder until the remainder is zero.

children.title: Extended Euclidean algorithm
children.definition: Also finds the coefficients x and y such that ax + by equals the gcd, which gives modular inverses.

children.title: Finding modular inverses
children.definition: The inverse of a modulo m exists when gcd is 1 and is found by the extended Euclidean algorithm.

children.title: Complexity of integer algorithms
children.definition: Bit operations count for addition, multiplication and division, and the running times of gcd computations.

children.title: Linear Diophantine equations
children.definition: Equations of the form ax + by = c are solvable exactly when gcd divides c.

card.explanation: Computers hold integers in base two, and converting between bases uses expansion on one side and repeated division on the other. The Euclidean algorithm finds the gcd by replacing the pair with the divisor and the remainder until the remainder is zero. The extended version also records the coefficients x and y with a x plus b y equal to the gcd. Those coefficients give the modular inverse of a, which exists whenever the gcd is one. The same condition decides a linear Diophantine equation, which is solvable exactly when the gcd of a and b divides c.
card.example: For 48 and 18: 48 is 2 times 18 plus 12, then 18 is 1 times 12 plus 6. Then 12 is 2 times 6 plus 0, so the gcd is 6.

quiz.q: What does the Euclidean algorithm compute?
quiz.why: It replaces the pair by the divisor and remainder repeatedly, and the last non-zero remainder is the gcd.

quiz.q: What extra output does the extended Euclidean algorithm give?
options: The coefficients x and y with a x plus b y equal to the gcd
quiz.why: Those coefficients are what produce a modular inverse when the gcd is 1.

quiz.q: When does a have an inverse modulo m?
options: When the gcd of a and m is 1
quiz.why: Being coprime to m is exactly the condition, and the extended Euclidean algorithm finds the inverse.

quiz.q: Which statement about integer algorithms is NOT correct?
options: A linear Diophantine equation needs the gcd to divide the constant
The Euclidean algorithm needs the prime factorisation first
The Euclidean algorithm ends when the remainder is zero
quiz.why: The Euclidean algorithm needs no factorisation, which is why it stays fast on very large numbers.

quiz.q: When is a x + b y = c solvable in integers?
options: Only when a and b are prime
When the gcd of a and b divides c
quiz.why: The gcd divides the left side whatever x and y are, so it has to divide c as well.

card.examTip: Show one Euclidean run as three division lines, then state two conditions: gcd 1 for an inverse, and gcd divides c for a Diophantine equation.

topics.title: Primes and Greatest Common Divisor
topics.definition: A prime has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself, and the gcd is the largest common divisor.

children.title: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic
children.definition: Every integer greater than 1 factors uniquely into primes up to order.

children.title: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic applications
children.definition: Finding gcd and lcm from prime factorisations.

children.title: Relatively prime numbers
children.definition: Two integers whose gcd is 1; pairwise relatively prime sets are used in number theory and cryptography.

children.title: Least common multiple
children.definition: The smallest positive integer divisible by both numbers, equal to a times b divided by gcd.

children.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes and trial division
children.definition: Methods for listing or testing primes; trial division needs checking divisors up to the square root.

children.title: Mersenne and Fermat primes
children.definition: Primes of the form 2 to the p minus 1 and Fermat numbers, with a role in primality testing.

card.explanation: A prime is an integer greater than one whose only positive divisors are one and itself. The fundamental theorem of arithmetic says every integer greater than one factors into primes in exactly one way, up to the order. That uniqueness is what lets the gcd and the lcm be read straight off the two factorisations. Two numbers are relatively prime when their gcd is one, and the lcm can be found from the product divided by the gcd. The sieve of Eratosthenes lists primes by crossing out multiples, and trial division tests one number by trying divisors up to its square root.
card.example: 12 is 2 squared times 3 and 18 is 2 times 3 squared. The gcd is 6 and the lcm is 36, read off the two factorisations.

quiz.q: What does the fundamental theorem of arithmetic state?
options: Every integer greater than 1 factors uniquely into primes
quiz.why: Existence and uniqueness of the prime factorisation is the content of the theorem.

quiz.q: How is the lcm found from the product of two numbers?
quiz.why: The gcd and lcm satisfy a times b equals gcd times lcm, so dividing gives the lcm.

quiz.q: Up to what value must trial division test divisors?
options: The square root of the number
quiz.why: If a divisor above the square root existed, its partner below it would have been found first.

quiz.q: Which statement about primes is NOT correct?
options: The sieve of Eratosthenes lists primes by crossing out multiples
A prime has exactly two positive divisors
Two numbers with gcd 1 are relatively prime
quiz.why: One is excluded by definition, because including it would break unique factorisation.

quiz.q: What form does a Mersenne prime have?
quiz.why: Mersenne primes are one less than a power of two, and the largest known primes are of this form.

card.examTip: Write the prime factorisations of two numbers, read off the gcd and lcm, then add the square root rule for trial division.

topics.title: Congruences and Classical Theorems
topics.definition: Congruence equations and famous theorems make computation with large numbers practical.

children.title: Systems of linear congruences
children.definition: Solved by substitution or by the Chinese remainder theorem.

children.title: Chinese remainder theorem
children.definition: A system of congruences with pairwise relatively prime moduli has a unique solution modulo their product.

children.title: Fermat little theorem
children.definition: If p is prime and a is not divisible by p then a to the p minus 1 is congruent to 1 mod p.

children.title: Euler theorem and totient
children.definition: Generalises Fermat with the totient phi, which counts integers up to n that are coprime to n.

children.title: Applications to cryptography
children.definition: RSA uses modular exponentiation, the totient function and large primes for public key encryption.

card.explanation: A system of linear congruences can be solved by substitution, or in one step by the Chinese remainder theorem. That theorem says a system whose moduli are pairwise relatively prime has a unique solution modulo their product. Fermat's little theorem says a to the p minus one is congruent to one modulo p. It needs p to be prime and not a divisor of a. Euler's theorem replaces p minus one with the totient phi of n, which counts the numbers up to n that are coprime to n. Both results are what make RSA work, because they let a huge exponent be reduced to a small one.
card.example: To find the last digit of 3 to the 100, work modulo 10. The powers of 3 repeat with period four, and 100 is a multiple of 4, so the answer is 1.

quiz.q: What does the Chinese remainder theorem require of the moduli?
options: They must be pairwise relatively prime
quiz.why: Pairwise coprime moduli give one solution modulo the product of all of them.

quiz.q: What does Fermat's little theorem say when p is prime and does not divide a?
options: a to the p is congruent to a mod p
a to the p minus 1 is congruent to 1 mod p
a is congruent to p mod a
a squared is congruent to 1 mod p
quiz.why: That is the classic form, and it is Euler's theorem with phi of p equal to p minus 1.

quiz.q: What does the totient phi of n count?
options: The integers up to n that are coprime to n
quiz.why: Phi of n is the size of the multiplicative group modulo n, which is why it appears in Euler's theorem.

quiz.q: Which statement about these theorems is NOT correct?
options: Euler's theorem generalises Fermat's little theorem
The Chinese remainder theorem gives a unique solution modulo the product
Fermat's little theorem needs p to be prime
RSA uses the totient because phi is easy to compute for any n
quiz.why: Computing phi is easy only when the factorisation is known, and that difficulty is what keeps RSA safe.

quiz.q: For a prime p, what is phi of p?
quiz.why: Every number from 1 to p minus 1 is coprime to a prime, so the count is p minus 1.

card.examTip: Write the three theorems with their exact conditions, then add one line on how RSA uses the totient and large primes.

topics.title: Groups
topics.definition: A group is a set with one binary operation that is associative, has an identity and gives every element an inverse.

children.title: Definition and axioms
children.definition: Closure, associativity, identity element and inverse element define a group.

children.title: Abelian group
children.definition: A group in which the operation is also commutative.

children.title: Examples of groups
children.definition: Integers under addition, non-zero rationals under multiplication and symmetries of a figure under composition.

children.title: Order of a group and of an element
children.definition: The number of elements in the group, and the smallest positive n with a to the n equal to the identity.

children.title: Subgroups
children.definition: A subset that is itself a group under the same operation, tested by closure and inverse conditions.

children.title: Permutation groups and symmetries
children.definition: Groups whose elements are bijections of a set, and the dihedral groups of polygons.

card.explanation: A group is a set with one operation satisfying four axioms: closure, associativity, an identity element and an inverse for every element. When the operation is also commutative the group is called abelian. The integers under addition form a group, and so do the non-zero rationals under multiplication. The order of a group is the number of elements in it. The order of an element is the smallest power that returns it to the identity. A subgroup is a subset that is a group in its own right under the same operation.
card.example: The integers under addition form a group with identity 0 and inverse minus n. The integers under multiplication do not, because 2 has no inverse that is still an integer.

quiz.q: Which four axioms define a group?
quiz.why: Commutativity is not required, and it is what makes an abelian group a special case.

quiz.q: What is a group whose operation is commutative called?
quiz.why: Abelian groups satisfy a times b equals b times a in addition to the four group axioms.

quiz.q: Which statement about groups is NOT correct?
options: Permutations of a set form a group under composition
The integers under addition form a group
The non-zero rationals under multiplication form a group
The integers under multiplication form a group
quiz.why: Most integers have no multiplicative inverse that is an integer, so the inverse axiom fails.

quiz.q: What is the order of an element a in a group?
options: The smallest positive n with a to the n equal to the identity
The number of subgroups containing a
The number of elements in the group
quiz.why: If no such power exists the element has infinite order, as in the integers under addition.

quiz.q: What must a subgroup satisfy?
options: Contain the identity and be closed under the operation and inverses
Contain every element of the group
quiz.why: Those conditions are exactly what makes the subset a group under the same operation.

card.examTip: State the four axioms, name one abelian and one non-abelian example, then give the subgroup test.

topics.title: Cyclic Groups and Homomorphism
topics.definition: A cyclic group is generated by one element, and a homomorphism is a structure preserving map between groups.

children.title: Cyclic group
children.definition: Every element is a power of a single generator g, such as the integers under addition with generator 1.

children.title: Generators and order
children.definition: The order of a cyclic group equals the order of its generator, and subgroups of cyclic groups are cyclic.

children.title: Group homomorphism
children.definition: A map f with f of a times b equal to f of a times f of b, preserving the operation.

children.title: Kernel and image
children.definition: The set mapping to the identity and the set of all images, both of which are subgroups.

children.title: Isomorphism
children.definition: A bijective homomorphism, which means the two groups are structurally the same.

children.title: Properties of homomorphisms
children.definition: Order preservation, the kernel as a normal subgroup and the first isomorphism theorem.

card.explanation: A cyclic group is one where every element is a power of a single generator g. The integers under addition are cyclic with generator 1, because every integer is a multiple of 1. In a finite cyclic group the order of the group equals the order of its generator, and every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic. A homomorphism is a map that respects the operation, so f of a times b equals f of a times f of b. Its kernel is everything that maps to the identity, and its image is everything that is reached; both are subgroups.
card.example: The integers modulo 6 under addition are cyclic, generated by 1. The element 2 generates only 0, 2 and 4, so it generates a proper subgroup.

quiz.q: What makes a group cyclic?
options: It has a finite number of elements
Every element is a power of one generator
quiz.why: One element and its powers produce the whole group, which is what generated means here.

quiz.q: What condition must a homomorphism satisfy?
options: f of a times b equals f of a times f of b
quiz.why: Preserving the operation is the definition; being one to one or onto is an extra property.

quiz.q: What is the kernel of a homomorphism?
options: The set of elements mapping to the identity
The set of elements of order two
quiz.why: The kernel measures how much the map collapses, and it is always a subgroup of the domain.

quiz.q: Which statement about cyclic groups is NOT correct?
options: The order of a finite cyclic group equals the order of its generator
Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic
The integers under addition are cyclic with generator 1
quiz.why: The integers under addition are an infinite cyclic group, so finiteness is not part of the definition.

quiz.q: What is an isomorphism?
options: A map that reverses the operation
A homomorphism with a trivial kernel
quiz.why: A bijective homomorphism preserves the structure both ways, so the groups differ only in names.

card.examTip: Give the definition of a cyclic group with one example, then state the homomorphism condition and name the kernel and image.

topics.title: Cosets, Normal Subgroups and Lagrange Theorem
topics.definition: Cosets split a group into equal sized blocks, and Lagrange theorem relates their size to the group order.

children.title: Left and right cosets
children.definition: Sets aH or Ha formed by multiplying a fixed element with every element of a subgroup.

children.title: Coset properties
children.definition: Cosets of a subgroup partition the group and all have the same size as the subgroup.

children.title: Index of a subgroup
children.definition: The number of distinct cosets, equal to the order of the group divided by the order of the subgroup.

children.title: Lagrange theorem
children.definition: The order of a subgroup divides the order of the finite group, so the order of every element divides the group order.

children.title: Normal subgroup
children.definition: A subgroup with aH equal to Ha for every a, which is exactly what allows a quotient group to be formed.

children.title: Quotient group and simple groups
children.definition: A quotient group is formed from the cosets of a normal subgroup; simple groups have no proper non-trivial normal subgroup.

card.explanation: A coset is one element multiplied by every element of a subgroup H, written aH on the left or Ha on the right. The cosets of H partition the group into blocks, and every block has exactly the size of H. The number of blocks is the index of H, which is the group order divided by the subgroup order. Lagrange's theorem says the order of a subgroup divides the order of the group, so the order of every element divides it too. A subgroup is normal when aH equals Ha for every a, and only then can the cosets be made into a quotient group.
card.example: In a group of order 12, a subgroup can only have order 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12. A subgroup of order 5 is impossible, because 5 does not divide 12.

quiz.q: What does Lagrange's theorem state?
options: The order of a subgroup divides the order of the group
quiz.why: The cosets have equal size and partition the group, so the group order is a multiple of the subgroup order.

quiz.q: A group has order 12. Which of these cannot be the order of a subgroup?
quiz.why: Lagrange's theorem allows only divisors of 12, and 5 is not one of them.

quiz.q: Which statement about cosets is NOT correct?
options: The number of cosets is called the index
Two cosets are either disjoint or they overlap partly
Cosets of a subgroup partition the group
All cosets of a subgroup have the same size
quiz.why: Two cosets are either identical or completely disjoint, which is what makes them a partition.

quiz.q: When is a subgroup called normal?
options: When aH equals Ha for every element a
quiz.why: Equal left and right cosets are what let a well defined quotient group be built from them.

quiz.q: What is a simple group?
options: A group of prime order with no operation
A group with no proper non-trivial normal subgroup
quiz.why: Simple groups are the building blocks, because they cannot be broken into a smaller quotient.

card.examTip: State Lagrange's theorem, give the divisor example, then define a normal subgroup with the aH equals Ha test.

topics.title: Rings and Fields
topics.definition: A ring has two operations with addition forming a group and multiplication distributing over it, and a field adds division.

children.title: Ring definition
children.definition: An abelian group under addition with an associative multiplication that distributes over addition.

children.title: Commutative ring and unity
children.definition: A ring where multiplication is commutative, with or without a multiplicative identity element.

children.title: Integral domain
children.definition: A commutative ring with unity and no zero divisors, so cancellation works.

children.title: Field definition and examples
children.definition: A commutative ring with unity in which every non-zero element has an inverse; rationals, reals and integers modulo a prime are fields.

children.title: Characteristic of a ring
children.definition: The smallest positive n with n times 1 equal to 0, which is 0, a prime or a composite.

children.title: Polynomial rings and applications
children.definition: Rings of polynomials and their use in coding theory and cryptography; finite fields underlie AES and error correcting codes.

card.explanation: A ring carries two operations: it is an abelian group under addition, and multiplication is associative and distributes over addition. A commutative ring with unity is one where multiplication commutes and there is a multiplicative identity. An integral domain adds the rule that there are no zero divisors, so a product can only be zero when one factor is. A field goes further and gives every non-zero element an inverse; the rationals, the reals and the integers modulo a prime are all fields. The characteristic is the smallest number of times the identity must be added to itself to reach zero.
card.example: The integers form an integral domain but not a field, because 2 has no integer inverse. The integers modulo 7 do form a field, because every non-zero class has an inverse.

quiz.q: What extra property makes a ring a field?
options: Every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse
quiz.why: Commutativity and associativity are already assumed; inverses for every non-zero element is the step up.

quiz.q: What is an integral domain?
options: A ring where every element has an inverse
A commutative ring with unity and no zero divisors
quiz.why: No zero divisors means a product of non-zero elements is never zero, so cancellation works.

quiz.q: Which of these is a field?
quiz.why: A prime modulus gives a field, because every non-zero class is coprime to 7 and has an inverse.

quiz.q: Which statement about rings is NOT correct?
options: A field has no zero divisors
A ring is an abelian group under addition
Every ring has a multiplicative identity
quiz.why: Unity is an extra condition; rings without it are valid and are called rings without unity.

quiz.q: What is the characteristic of a ring?
options: The smallest n with n times the identity equal to zero
The order of its multiplicative group
The number of elements in it
quiz.why: If no such n exists the characteristic is zero, which is the case for the integers and the reals.

card.examTip: Give the definitions in a chain: ring, commutative ring with unity, integral domain, field. Add one example at each step.

topics.title: Basics of Counting
topics.definition: Counting determines the size of a set without listing all its elements.

children.title: Product rule
children.definition: If one task has m outcomes and a second has n, the pair has m times n outcomes.

children.title: Sum rule
children.definition: If two cases cannot happen together with m and n outcomes, the total is m + n.

children.title: Subtraction (inclusion exclusion) rule
children.definition: For overlapping cases, the total is m + n minus the number of common outcomes.

children.title: Tree diagrams
children.definition: A branching diagram that shows all outcomes of a sequence of choices.

children.title: Counting with sets and functions
children.definition: Counting subsets, functions between finite sets and the number of injective functions.

card.explanation: Counting finds how many outcomes there are without writing them all down. The product rule says that two independent choices with m and n outcomes give m times n outcomes together. The sum rule says that two cases which cannot happen together with m and n outcomes give m plus n. When the cases overlap, the subtraction rule removes the double count, which is the inclusion exclusion idea. A tree diagram draws the choices as branches, so the count is the number of leaves. The same rules count subsets, functions between finite sets and injective functions.
card.example: A meal has 3 starters and 4 main courses, giving 3 times 4 which is 12 combinations. Adding 2 desserts makes it 3 times 4 times 2, which is 24.

quiz.q: A code has 2 letters followed by 3 digits. With 26 letters and 10 digits, how many codes are there?
quiz.why: The product rule multiplies the number of choices at each of the five positions.

quiz.q: A student can take one of 4 maths courses or one of 3 physics courses, but not both. How many choices?
quiz.why: The cases cannot happen together, so the sum rule applies and the counts are added.

quiz.q: Which statement about counting rules is NOT correct?
options: The product rule applies to a sequence of choices
The sum rule applies to cases that cannot overlap
The subtraction rule removes outcomes counted twice
A tree diagram counts by multiplying the number of levels
quiz.why: A tree diagram counts by the number of leaves, which is the product of the branch counts per level.

quiz.q: How many functions are there from a set of 3 elements to a set of 5 elements?
quiz.why: Each of the 3 inputs may go to any of the 5 outputs, so the choices multiply to 5 cubed.

quiz.q: In a class of 30, 18 study maths and 12 study physics, and 5 study both. How many study at least one?
quiz.why: Inclusion exclusion gives 18 + 12 - 5, which is 25.

card.examTip: State the product and sum rule in one line each, then show the inclusion exclusion count with numbers.

topics.title: Pigeonhole Principle
topics.definition: If more items than boxes are placed into boxes, some box holds more than one item.

children.title: Simple pigeonhole principle
children.definition: Placing n + 1 objects into n boxes forces at least one box to hold two objects.

children.title: Generalised pigeonhole principle
children.definition: Placing N objects into k boxes forces some box to hold at least the ceiling of N divided by k objects.

children.title: Classical applications
children.definition: Among any 13 people two share a birth month, and among n + 1 integers chosen from 1 to 2n one divides another.

children.title: Subsequence and geometry applications
children.definition: Any sequence of n squared + 1 distinct numbers has an increasing or decreasing subsequence of length n + 1.

card.explanation: The pigeonhole principle is the simple fact that more objects than boxes forces a box to hold two. In its general form, placing N objects into k boxes forces some box to hold at least the ceiling of N divided by k objects. The point of the method is choosing the boxes well, because the statement you want follows from how you set them up. Among thirteen people two share a birth month, because there are only twelve months. Among n plus 1 integers chosen from 1 to 2n, one divides another, which is proved by stripping powers of two.
card.example: In any group of 367 people two share a birthday, because there are only 366 possible dates. No probability is needed to say this.

quiz.q: What does the simple pigeonhole principle say?
options: The boxes must be arranged in order
n objects in n boxes fill every box
n + 1 objects in n boxes force a box to hold two
quiz.why: One more object than there are boxes makes a shared box unavoidable.

quiz.q: What does the generalised principle guarantee when N objects go into k boxes?
options: Some box holds exactly N divided by k
Every box holds the same number
Some box holds at least the ceiling of N divided by k
quiz.why: The ceiling is needed because objects are whole, so the average is rounded up.

quiz.q: How many people guarantee that two share a birth month?
quiz.why: With 12 months, 13 people force a shared month by the pigeonhole principle.

quiz.q: Which statement about the pigeonhole principle is NOT correct?
options: Choosing the boxes well is the main skill
It proves that some box holds at most the average
It applies to any sequence of n squared + 1 distinct numbers
It proves existence without identifying which box is shared
quiz.why: The principle guarantees a box holding at least the average, never at most it.

quiz.q: Any sequence of n squared + 1 distinct numbers must contain:
options: An increasing or decreasing subsequence of length n + 1
quiz.why: That is the classic subsequence application, proved by attaching a pair of lengths to each term.

card.examTip: State both forms of the principle, then give two applications: the shared birth month and the subsequence result.

topics.title: Permutations and Combinations
topics.definition: A permutation counts ordered arrangements and a combination counts unordered selections.

children.title: Permutations without repetition
children.definition: The number of ways to arrange r items chosen from n is n factorial divided by (n minus r) factorial.

children.title: Permutations with repetition
children.definition: Arrangements when items may repeat are n to the power r.

children.title: Circular permutations
children.definition: Arrangements around a circle number (n minus 1) factorial because rotations are the same.

children.title: Combinations
children.definition: The number of r element subsets of an n element set is n factorial over r factorial times (n minus r) factorial.

children.title: Combinations with repetition
children.definition: Distributions of identical objects into distinct boxes number C of (n plus r minus 1) choose r.

children.title: Permutations and combinations with restrictions
children.definition: Cases with adjacent items, no two together, or fixed positions handled by first arranging the restricted items.

card.explanation: A permutation counts arrangements where the order matters, and a combination counts selections where it does not. Arranging r items chosen from n gives n factorial divided by n minus r factorial. When items may repeat, the count is n to the power r. Around a circle the count is n minus 1 factorial, because rotating the circle changes nothing. Choosing r items from n without caring about order gives n factorial over r factorial times n minus r factorial, read as n choose r. When repetition is allowed in a selection, the count becomes n plus r minus 1 choose r.
card.example: Five books can be arranged on a shelf in 5 factorial, which is 120 ways. Choosing 3 of them to take home gives 5 choose 3, which is 10 ways, because the packing order does not matter.

quiz.q: How many ways can 3 books be chosen from 5 when order does not matter?
quiz.why: It is a combination, 5 choose 3, which is 5 factorial over 3 factorial times 2 factorial, giving 10.

quiz.q: How many ways can 5 people sit around a round table?
quiz.why: Rotations are the same arrangement, so one seat is fixed and the other 4 are arranged.

quiz.q: Which statement is NOT correct?
options: A circular permutation of n objects is n minus 1 factorial
The number of arrangements of r from n equals n choose r
quiz.why: Arrangements use n factorial over n minus r factorial, while n choose r ignores the order.

quiz.q: How many 4 digit PINs can be made from 10 digits if repetition is allowed?
quiz.why: Each of the four positions has 10 choices, so the count is 10 to the power 4.

quiz.q: In how many ways can the letters of the word CAT be arranged?
quiz.why: There are 3 distinct letters, so the count is 3 factorial, which is 6.

card.examTip: Write the four formulas side by side: permutation, with repetition, circular and combination. Note which divide by a factorial and why.

topics.title: Binomial Coefficients and the Binomial Theorem
topics.definition: Binomial coefficients count selections and appear as the coefficients in the expansion of a power of a binomial.

children.title: Binomial theorem
children.definition: The expansion of (x plus y) to the n as a sum of C(n, k) times x to the n minus k times y to the k.

children.title: Pascal triangle and Pascal identity
children.definition: Each entry is the sum of the two above it, which is the identity C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k).

children.title: Useful identities
children.definition: C(n, k) = C(n, n-k), the sum of all C(n, k) is 2 to the n, and Vandermonde identity.

children.title: Multinomial coefficients and theorem
children.definition: Counting arrangements of objects of several types, and the expansion of a sum of several terms.

children.title: Applications of counting
children.definition: Probability of card and dice outcomes, password strength, seat allocation and algorithm analysis.

card.explanation: The binomial theorem expands x plus y to the n into a sum of terms. Each term is n choose k times x to the n minus k times y to the k. The coefficients are the entries of Pascal's triangle, where each entry is the sum of the two above it. That is Pascal's identity in symbols: n choose k equals n minus 1 choose k minus 1 plus n minus 1 choose k. Two identities are used constantly: symmetry, and a row sum of 2 to the n. Symmetry says n choose k equals n choose n minus k. The multinomial theorem does the same job for a sum of several terms.
card.example: Row 4 of Pascal's triangle is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, which are the coefficients in the expansion of x plus y to the 4.

quiz.q: What is the sum of all binomial coefficients n choose k for a fixed n?
quiz.why: Putting x and y both equal to 1 in the binomial theorem gives 1 plus 1 to the n, which is 2 to the n.

quiz.q: Which identity does Pascal's triangle show?
options: n choose k equals n choose n minus k
n choose k equals C(n-1,k-1) + C(n-1,k)
The sum of a row is 2 to the n
quiz.why: Each entry is the sum of the two entries above it, which is exactly Pascal's identity.

quiz.q: What is the coefficient of x squared y squared in the expansion of (x + y) to the 4?
quiz.why: It is 4 choose 2, which is 6, the middle entry of row 4 of Pascal's triangle.

quiz.q: Which statement about binomial coefficients is NOT correct?
options: n choose k equals n choose n minus k
The rows of Pascal's triangle are symmetric
n choose k is largest only when k equals n
quiz.why: The largest entries sit in the middle of a row, and n choose n is 1, the smallest value.

quiz.q: Which theorem expands a power of a sum of several terms?
quiz.why: Multinomial coefficients count arrangements of objects of several types, generalising the binomial case.

card.examTip: Write the binomial theorem in sigma form, draw four rows of Pascal's triangle, then state the symmetry and sum identities.
